title: Do you play the story, or skip to the decision?
audience: Dinis: it is his own experience as the user, not a reserved decision
summary: Every decision brief can play its story first or open on the decision. Which should be the default, and for which decisions? One decision for Dinis, from sherpa.d's reading of his words.

beats.narration: You asked whether a brief should play its story, or skip to the decision, and wanted to decide it from an animation. Only your own use can show which is right, so it is asked of you.

visual.text: Story first, or the decision first?

beats.narration: Two paths lead into the same choice. You notice a decision, open its brief, and either let the story play before the decision, or skip straight to it. Then you answer and get a receipt.

Option A, today: the story plays first and the decision comes at the end. Context is always seen once, but the story costs time when your answer is a plain yes, and it is the same length for a small yes and for a key decision.

left.title: A. Story first (today)
points: Does well: context seen once; matches your 12:40 word
Does badly: slow when the answer is yes

right.title: B. Decision first
points: Does well: fastest for routine yeses
Does badly: context easy to skip when it was needed

beats.narration: Option C, recommended: it depends on the kind of decision. Routine ones open on the decision. Your reserved ones, money, law, brand, people, keys and what RiskMandate is, play the story first.

items: Routine: opens on the decision, story one tap away
Reserved (money, law, brand, people, keys, what RiskMandate is): story first
Needs each decision tagged routine or reserved, checked by helm.d

beats.narration: How we will know: your own use. Which stories you play to the end, which you skip, and which decisions you answer without playing. A week of that settles it better than any review.
One caveat. This is sherpa.d's reading of your words and two pages. It is not a test with you, and the diagram is a sketch, not a design.
